newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - Business as usual in post-handover HK.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - Business as usual in post-handover HK.

text.p: Hong Kong will see changes in 1997 when it returns to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30, but analysts say it should be business as usual for both investors and the territory after the handover.

"We do not expect the Hong Kong economy to be impacted by post-1997 blues, as confidence about the territory's post-1997 prospects remains strong and the economy is on a cyclical upswing," Salomon Brothers said in a recent economic report.
The economic and investment implications of Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule have been the topic of much discussion.

Key elements which will determine the post-handover picture include the selection on December 11 of shipping tycoon Tung Chee-hwa as the territory's first post-colonial leader and the naming of the 60-member provisional legislature on Saturday.
Tung's selection was generally seen as positive by both the local and international business communities because of his business experience and good relations with Beijing.

Merrill Lynch said investors should remain overweight in Hong Kong equities next year, forecasting 15 percent earnings per share growth for Hang Seng Index companies and fair valuation for the blue-chip barometer at 15,000 points.
The Hang Seng Index closed at 13,131.41 points on Friday.

Sino-British relations over the handover have moved down a "reasonably bumpy road" but the outcome has already been factored into the local market, Merrill political analyst Richard Margolis said last week.
"There is a constancy about our political risk and vulnerability," Margolis said at a presentation of Merrill's Asia-Pacific outlook. "Politics, in a sense, is irrelevant."

There was nothing in the transfer of sovereignty to change Merrill's forecasts for 1997 of 5.2 percent economic growth, a recovery in corporate core earnings and a rise in the stock market, Margolis said.
Other analysts said the handover had relatively little to do with the performance of Hong Kong's stock market.

"Although there is a tendency to link the performance of the local stock market to confidence in the 1997 transition, this is a mistake," Political & Economic Risk Consultancy Ltd said in its December outlook on Hong Kong.
"The performance of the U.S. market is much more directly relevant, so that the most likely cause of a downturn will not be a local political development but a sharp correction in the U.S. market."
Salomon said it was bullish on Hong Kong, forecasting gross domestic product growth of 5.5 percent in both 1997 and 1998 from an estimated 5.0 percent this year and 4.8 percent in 1995.
Salomon said it based its stance on expectations of a steady recovery in consumer spending, the likelihood of stable U.S. short-term interest rates and the continuing recovery of the Chinese economy.

The worst-case scenario, Merrill's Margolis said, would be Chinese leaders withdrawing support for the large measure of autonomy Hong Kong has been promised after the handover. But he said a change in the territory's "separate status" was unlikely.

Hong Kong's post-handover administration will also have to deal with issues such as the rule of law, freedom of the press and assimilation of the territory's largely free economic system with that of its new sovereign, analysts said.
But Merrill said investors would be looking beyond the handover to the basics.

"By the time the stock market re-opens on Friday, July 4 ... we shall again need to focus our attention on the fundamentals -- the future direction of U.S. interest rates, and China's economic performance and earnings growth," it said.
